criticalConfirmed.detail: 去夏桓沖送死 is hostile rhetoric that Huan Chong came courting death; it does not report his death. Extraction already removed the death claim (c0616 is failed-attack attestation); AD 384 year remains chronology-blocked.
牢之追垂，連戰皆敗 — Laozhi loses successive pursuits. Idiomatic had reversed the outcome. Extraction event c0689 already rewritten; Western year on c0690 remains chronology-blocked.

repairs.before: After Shi Hu had invaded and withdrawn, Murong Huang still intended to expand his domain and sent the general Deng Heng with tens of thousands of men to camp at Le'an, making ready to attack and take new territory.
repairs.after: After Shi Hu had invaded and withdrawn, he still intended to annex Yan and sent the general Deng Heng with tens of thousands of men to camp at Le'an, making ready to attack and take new territory.
repairs.reason: Chinese keeps 石季龍 as subject of 猶有兼併之志 and 遣將鄧恆; Deng Heng is Shi Hu's general, not Murong Huang's.
repairs.authorReason: The subject of 猶有兼併之志 and 遣將鄧恆 is 石季龍 (Shi Hu); Deng Heng was his general, not Murong Huang's.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 猶有兼併之志，遣將鄧恆

repairs.before: Murong Gen urged Jun, "What the prince says comes once in an age and must not be missed."
repairs.after: Muyu Gen urged Jun, "What the prince says comes once in an age and must not be missed."
repairs.reason: The speaker is 慕輿根 (surname Muyu), not Murong Gen.
repairs.authorReason: The Chinese name is 慕輿根, surname Muyu, not Murong.

repairs.before: Murong Gen said to Jun, "The prince's words are a once-in-a-thousand-years moment and must not be lost."
repairs.after: Muyu Gen said to Jun, "The prince's words are a once-in-a-thousand-years moment and must not be lost."
repairs.reason: Parallel literal field: 慕輿根 is Muyu Gen.
repairs.authorReason: The Chinese name is 慕輿根, surname Muyu, not Murong.

repairs.before: At that time Murong Wei held the throne and Murong Ke served as Grand Preceptor.
repairs.after: At that time Murong Wei held the throne and Murong Ke served as Grand Steward.
repairs.reason: 太宰 is Grand Steward, not Grand Preceptor.
repairs.authorReason: 太宰 is Grand Steward (Taizai), not Grand Preceptor.

repairs.before: Chui told Rang, "I owe the emperor a boundless debt; I wished to send the Marquis of Changle with all his men to the capital, then restore my house and live at peace with Qin.
repairs.after: Chui told Rang, "I owe the emperor a boundless debt; I wished to send the Duke of Changle with all his men to the capital, then restore my house and live at peace with Qin.
repairs.reason: 長樂公 is Duke of Changle (Fu Pi), not a marquis.
repairs.authorReason: 長樂公 is the Duke (公) of Changle, Fu Pi's title, not a marquis.

repairs.before: The Marquis of Changle is the emperor's heir, his virtue beyond Tang and Wei, the pillar east of the mountains—he will not meekly yield you a hundred cities!
repairs.after: The Duke of Changle is the emperor's eldest son, his virtue beyond Tang and Wei, the pillar east of the mountains—he will not meekly yield you a hundred cities!
repairs.reason: 長樂公 is Duke of Changle; 元子 is eldest son.
repairs.authorReason: 長樂公 is Duke of Changle; 元子 means eldest son.

repairs.before: Just then Fu Hui reported that the Dingling leader Zhai Bin had raised a host against Luoyang; Fu Pi told Chui, "The Bin brothers, exploiting our recent setback, dare rise in violence; mother and son together are a hard match—only your brilliance can break them.
repairs.after: Just then Fu Jian's general Fu Hui reported that the Dingling leader Zhai Bin had raised a host against Luoyang; Fu Pi told Chui, "Bin and his brothers, exploiting our recent setback, dare rise in violence; a mother-and-son force is a hard match—only your brilliance can break them.
repairs.reason: 堅將苻暉 marks Fu Hui as Fu Jian's general; 斌兄弟 is Bin and his brothers.
repairs.authorReason: 堅將苻暉 identifies Fu Hui as Fu Jian's general; 斌兄弟 is Bin and his brothers.

repairs.before: I was ordered north and bound by the Marquis of Changle.
repairs.after: I was ordered north and bound by the Duke of Changle.
repairs.reason: 長樂 here is Fu Pi as Duke of Changle.
repairs.authorReason: 長樂 here is Fu Pi, Duke (公) of Changle.

repairs.before: I asked the Marquis of Changle to send all his men to the emperor and release them with honor; Pi clung to his obstinacy and would not bend.
repairs.after: I asked the Duke of Changle to send all his men to the emperor and release them with honor; Pi clung to his obstinacy and would not bend.
repairs.reason: 長樂公 is Duke of Changle.
repairs.authorReason: 長樂公 is Duke of Changle.

repairs.before: At Luoyang the Plain Duke Fu Hui would not trust me.
repairs.after: At Luoyang Fu Hui, Duke of Pingyuan, would not trust me.
repairs.reason: 平原公 is Duke of Pingyuan, not a literal "Plain Duke".
repairs.authorReason: 平原公 is the title Duke of Pingyuan, not a 'Plain Duke'.

repairs.before: Only for Changle and the Plain Duke, still young when they met you in the Two Capitals—we regret their counsel was not to our mind; that is all."
repairs.after: Only for Changle and Pingyuan, still young when they met you in the Two Capitals—we regret their counsel was not to our mind; that is all."
repairs.reason: 平原 is the Pingyuan fief title paired with Changle.
repairs.authorReason: 平原 is Fu Hui's fief Pingyuan.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 但長樂、平原以未立之年

repairs.before: Chui smiled and said, "What can this boy do? I will be your butcher and kill him."
repairs.after: Chui smiled and said, "What can this brat do? I shall kill him for you all."
repairs.reason: 堅子 is contemptuous "brat"; 為卿等殺之 means kill him for you all, not "be your butcher"/Fu Jian.
repairs.authorReason: 堅子 is a contemptuous 'brat', not Fu Jian.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 堅子何能為，吾今為卿等殺之

repairs.before: Yong thought it a feint and pulled all his men back to guard Zhatai Pass.
repairs.after: Yong thought it a feint and pulled all his men back to guard the Taihang and Zhi passes.
repairs.reason: 太行軹關 names the Taihang passes and Zhi Pass.
repairs.authorReason: 太行軹關 refers to the Taihang passes and Zhi Pass, not a 'Zhatai Pass'.

repairs.before: At that time Murong Wei succeeded to the false throne and Murong Ke was Grand Preceptor.
repairs.after: At that time Murong Wei succeeded to the false throne and Murong Ke was Grand Steward.
repairs.reason: Parallel literal: 太宰 is Grand Steward.
repairs.authorReason: 太宰 is Grand Steward, not Grand Preceptor; this is the parallel-field correction to the existing idiomatic proposal.

repairs.before: Earlier, when Bao was at Chang'an, with Han Huang, Li Gen, and others he was at a banquet playing liubo; Bao sat upright and composed his appearance and swore, "The world says liubo has a god—is this empty talk!
repairs.after: Earlier, when Bao was at Chang'an, he attended a banquet with Han Huang, Li Gen, and others and played chupu; Bao sat upright, composed his expression, and swore, "The world says chupu has a god—is this empty talk!
repairs.reason: 摴蒱 is chupu; later 五木 confirms the gaming pieces.
repairs.authorReason: 摴蒱 is the game chupu, not liubo.

repairs.before: Earlier, while Bao was at Chang'an, he played liubo at a feast with Han Huang, Li Gen, and others; sitting rigidly upright he swore, "Men say the dice have a god—surely that is no idle tale!
repairs.after: Earlier, while Bao was at Chang'an, he played chupu at a feast with Han Huang, Li Gen, and others; sitting rigidly upright he swore, "Men say the gaming pieces have a god—surely that is no idle tale!
repairs.reason: Parallel idiomatic: 摴蒱 is chupu, not liubo.
repairs.authorReason: 摴蒱 is chupu; 五木 in s0075 confirms its five wooden gaming pieces, not liubo.

repairs.before: His men are tired and few—strike now and take him."
repairs.after: His generals are old and his soldiers weary—strike now and take him."
repairs.reason: 將老兵疲 means old generals and weary soldiers, not few men.
repairs.authorReason: 將老兵疲 says the generals are old and the soldiers weary; it does not say the men are few.

repairs.before: Chui refused, saying, "My father and I entrusted our lives to the Qin court; in peril we were saved, bearing the sovereign's unworldly grace and receiving the favor of renewed life—though called minister and ruler, our bond is as deep as father and son; how can we, for a small rift, harbor divided loyalties.
repairs.after: Chui refused, saying, "My son and I entrusted our lives to the Qin court; in peril we were saved, bearing the sovereign's unworldly grace and receiving the favor of renewed life—though called minister and ruler, our bond is as deep as father and son; how can we, for a small rift, harbor divided loyalties.
repairs.reason: In context of Chui's Qin refuge with his son, 吾父子 is "my son and I".
repairs.authorReason: 吾父子 means 'my son and I' here, not 'my father and I'; Chui and his son had taken refuge with Qin.

repairs.before: Chui declined: "My father and I cast our lot with Qin in mortal danger and were spared; we owe the emperor a grace beyond measure and life itself—though called subject and lord, our bond is that of father and son; how could a small quarrel make us waver in loyalty?
repairs.after: Chui declined: "My son and I cast our lot with Qin in mortal danger and were spared; we owe the emperor a grace beyond measure and life itself—though called subject and lord, our bond is that of father and son; how could a small quarrel make us waver in loyalty?
repairs.reason: Parallel idiomatic: 吾父子 is Chui and his son.
repairs.authorReason: 吾父子 denotes Chui and his son, not Chui and his father.

repairs.before: Chui led troops to Xingyang; in the eighth year of the Taiping reign of Emperor Xiaowu he styled himself Grand General, Grand Commander, and Prince of Yan, acting by imperial commission, and established the era name Yan Yuan.
repairs.after: Chui led troops to Xingyang; in the eighth year of the Taiyuan era he styled himself Grand General, Grand Commander, and Prince of Yan, acting by imperial commission, and established the era name Yan Yuan.
repairs.reason: 太元 is the Taiyuan era, not Taiping.
repairs.authorReason: 太元 is the Taiyuan era, not a Taiping reign.

repairs.before: Chui said to Rang, "I received the sovereign's unworldly grace and therefore wished to keep the Marquis of Changle safe, have him send all his host to the capital, and then restore the house and state, remaining forever Qin's neighbor in good faith.
repairs.after: Chui said to Rang, "I received the sovereign's unworldly grace and therefore wished to keep the Duke of Changle safe, have him send all his host to the capital, and then restore the house and state, remaining forever Qin's neighbor in good faith.
repairs.reason: Parallel literal: 長樂公 is Duke of Changle.
repairs.authorReason: 長樂公 is Duke of Changle; this supplies the literal-field counterpart to the existing idiomatic proposal.

repairs.before: The Princess of Changle is the sovereign's eldest son, his virtue surpassing Tang and Wei, holding the duty east of Shan—he is the court's bulwark; how can he meekly hand the general a hundred cities!
repairs.after: The Duke of Changle is the sovereign's eldest son, his virtue surpassing Tang and Wei, holding the duty east of Shan—he is the court's bulwark; how can he meekly hand the general a hundred cities!
repairs.reason: 長樂公 cannot be "Princess"; 元子 is eldest son.
repairs.authorReason: 長樂公 is Duke of Changle and 元子 explicitly says eldest son; 'Princess' contradicts both.

repairs.before: Last summer Huan Chong came to his death; in one plan it was like clouds dispersed; returning to attack Xiangcheng, captives and severed ears numbered in the tens of thousands—this is truly Your Majesty's divine calculation, and also your foolish servant's effect of forgetting death.
repairs.after: Last summer Huan Chong came courting death; at one stroke his forces dispersed like clouds; returning to attack Yuncheng, we took captives and severed ears by the tens of thousands—this was truly Your Majesty's divine calculation, and also the result of your foolish servant's disregard for death.
repairs.reason: 送死 is hostile rhetoric ("came courting death"), not a death report; 鄖城 is Yuncheng; 俘馘 are captives and severed ears.
repairs.authorReason: 送死 is hostile rhetoric for coming to court death, not a statement that Huan Chong died; 鄖城 is Yuncheng, not Xiangcheng, and 俘馘 distinguishes captives and severed ears.

repairs.before: Last summer Huan Chong died; our plans cleared like clouds; at Xiangcheng we took tens of thousands of heads—this was your divine strategy and my small share of dying for you.
repairs.after: Last summer Huan Chong came courting death; at one stroke his forces scattered like clouds; we then attacked Yuncheng and took tens of thousands of captives and severed ears—this was your divine strategy and my small share in risking death for you.
repairs.reason: Idiomatic false death and Xiangcheng/heads errors corrected against 送死 / 鄖城 / 俘馘.
repairs.authorReason: The sentence describes Huan Chong's failed attack, not his death; it names 鄖城 (Yuncheng) and 俘馘 (captives and severed ears), not Xiangcheng and heads alone.

repairs.before: Your servant received the edict to tour the north and was constrained by the Marquis of Changle.
repairs.after: Your servant received the edict to tour the north and was constrained by the Duke of Changle.
repairs.reason: Parallel literal: 長樂 is Duke of Changle.
repairs.authorReason: 長樂 refers to Fu Pi's title, Duke of Changle; this is the literal counterpart to the existing idiomatic proposal.

repairs.before: When I reached Luoyang, the Plain Duke Hui again would not trust or accept me.
repairs.after: When I reached Luoyang, Fu Hui, Duke of Pingyuan, again would not trust or accept me.
repairs.reason: Parallel literal: 平原公暉 is Fu Hui, Duke of Pingyuan.
repairs.authorReason: 平原公暉 is Fu Hui with the fief title Duke of Pingyuan, not a 'Plain Duke'; this parallels the existing idiomatic proposal.

repairs.before: I wished to have the Marquis of Changle send all his host to the rescue and dismiss them with ceremony, but Pi obstinately held the will of a common man and did not comprehend the principle of change.
repairs.after: I wished to have the Duke of Changle send all his host to the rescue and dismiss them with ceremony, but Pi obstinately held the will of a common man and did not comprehend the principle of change.
repairs.reason: Parallel literal: 長樂公 is Duke of Changle.
repairs.authorReason: 長樂公 is Duke of Changle; this is the literal counterpart to the existing idiomatic proposal.

repairs.before: We were about to entrust you with the office of chief minister and enfeoff you as marquis of a commandery, hoping broadly to cross hardship and respectfully repay your merit—why has Bo Yi suddenly destroyed his icy integrity and willow Hui instantly become a debauched man!
repairs.after: We were about to entrust you with the office of chief minister and enfeoff you as marquis of a commandery, hoping broadly to cross hardship and respectfully repay your merit—why has Bo Yi suddenly destroyed his icy integrity and Liuxia Hui instantly become a debauched man!
repairs.reason: 柳惠 abbreviates the exemplar Liuxia Hui, not "willow Hui".
repairs.authorReason: 柳惠 is the abbreviated name of the exemplar Liuxia Hui, not the phrase 'willow Hui'.

repairs.before: I would have made you chief minister and marquis of a commandery to repay your merit—why has Bo Yi shattered his honor and Liu Hui turned debauched!
repairs.after: I would have made you chief minister and marquis of a commandery to repay your merit—why has Bo Yi shattered his honor and Liuxia Hui turned debauched!
repairs.reason: Parallel idiomatic: 柳惠 is Liuxia Hui.
repairs.authorReason: 柳惠 refers to Liuxia Hui; the extraction itself canonically identifies p070 as Liuxia Hui.

repairs.before: Only the Marquis of Changle and the Plain Duke, in years not yet established, met you in the Two Capitals—we regret that their planning and conduct did not match Our heart; this is the only thing regretted."
repairs.after: Only the Duke of Changle and the Duke of Pingyuan, in years not yet established, met you in the Two Capitals—we regret that their planning and conduct did not match Our heart; this is the only thing regretted."
repairs.reason: Parallel literal: 長樂 and 平原 are duke-fief titles.
repairs.authorReason: 長樂 and 平原 are the fief titles Duke of Changle and Duke of Pingyuan; this is the literal counterpart to existing title repairs.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 但長樂、平原以未立之年

repairs.before: Bin's nephew Zhen fled north to Handan and marched on Ye to join Pi from within; Chui sent Bao and Murong Long to break him.
repairs.after: Bin's nephew Zhen fled north to Handan and marched on Ye, intending to coordinate with Pi from outside and inside; Chui sent Bao and Murong Long to break him.
repairs.reason: 欲與丕為內外之勢 is coordinated outside/inside posture, not joining Pi from within.
repairs.authorReason: 欲與丕為內外之勢 means Zhen outside and Fu Pi inside would form a coordinated external-internal position; Zhen was not joining Pi 'from within'.

repairs.before: Chui himself fled north from Xincheng; Laozhi pursued Chui and in successive battles all were defeats.
repairs.after: Chui fled north from Xincheng; Laozhi pursued him but was defeated in every successive battle.
repairs.reason: Subject continuity: 牢之追垂，連戰皆敗 — Laozhi loses the successive fights.
repairs.authorReason: 牢之 is the subject of 追 and remains the subject of 連戰皆敗; s0206 immediately continues with the Jin royal army's defeat.

repairs.before: Chui fled north; Laozhi pursued and defeated him again and again.
repairs.after: Chui fled north; Laozhi pursued but was defeated again and again.
repairs.reason: Idiomatic had reversed the outcome; Chinese says Laozhi was defeated again and again.
repairs.authorReason: The idiomatic translation reverses the outcome: 連戰皆敗 says Liu Laozhi lost the successive engagements.

repairs.before: The General Who Establishes the Commandery Xu Yan rebelled at Wuyi, drove and plundered more than four thousand men, and fled north to Youzhou.
repairs.after: The General Who Establishes the Standard Xu Yan rebelled at Wuyi, drove off and plundered more than four thousand people, and fled north to Youzhou.
repairs.reason: 建節將軍 uses 節 as the command standard/tally, not a commandery.
repairs.authorReason: 建節 is an official title involving the command standard 節, not a commandery.

repairs.before: Liao in terror sued for peace.
repairs.after: Liao in terror sent an envoy to request surrender.
repairs.reason: 遣使請降 is an envoy requesting surrender, not merely suing for peace.
repairs.authorReason: 遣使請降 explicitly says he sent an envoy to ask to surrender, not merely to seek peace.

repairs.before: Yong thought Chui was using a deceptive route to attack him and therefore gathered all his armies back to guard the Zhatai Pass at Huatai.
repairs.after: Yong thought Chui was attacking him by a deceptive route and therefore gathered all his armies back to guard the Taihang and Zhi passes.
repairs.reason: Parallel literal: 太行軹關 = Taihang and Zhi passes.
repairs.authorReason: 太行軹關 names the Taihang passes and Zhi Pass, not a 'Zhatai Pass at Huatai'; this supplies the literal counterpart to the existing idiomatic proposal.

repairs.before: Chui advanced the army entering from Tianjing Pass, reaching Hubei.
repairs.after: Chui advanced the army through Tianjing Pass and reached Hubi.
repairs.reason: 壺壁 is Hubi, not Hubei.
repairs.authorReason: 壺壁 is the place Hubi, not Hubei.

repairs.before: Chui entered by Tianjing Pass and reached Hubei.
repairs.after: Chui entered by Tianjing Pass and reached Hubi.
repairs.reason: Parallel idiomatic: 壺壁 is Hubi.
repairs.authorReason: 壺壁 is Hubi; s0258 repeats the same place.

repairs.before: Chui, ashamed and indignant, spat blood; because of this he took to his bed ill, riding in a litter he advanced.
repairs.after: Chui, ashamed and indignant, vomited blood; because of this he fell ill and advanced in a horse-drawn litter.
repairs.reason: 歐血/嘔血 is vomited blood; 馬輿 is a horse-drawn litter.
repairs.authorReason: 歐血 (嘔血) means vomited blood; 馬輿 is a horse-drawn carriage or litter, not an assertion that he rode while bedridden.

repairs.before: Chui, shamed and raging, coughed blood, fell ill, and was carried forward in a litter.
repairs.after: Chui, shamed and raging, vomited blood, fell ill, and was carried forward in a horse-drawn litter.
repairs.reason: Parallel idiomatic: vomited blood, not coughed blood.
repairs.authorReason: 歐血 (嘔血) is vomiting blood, not coughing blood.

repairs.before: Bao and the rest, reaching Yunzhong, heard Chui was dying and turned back.
repairs.after: Bao and the rest, reaching Yunzhong, heard Chui was ill and turned back.
repairs.reason: 聞垂疾 reports illness, not that Chui was dying.
repairs.authorReason: 聞垂疾 says they heard of Chui's illness; it does not say he was dying.

repairs.before: Taking his Left Chief Clerk Guan Wei of Ku Ruo, Right Chief Clerk Duan Chong, and Dragon-Charger Zhang Chong, together with the Administrator of Zhongshan Feng Heng, as Minister of the Imperial Secretariat; Murong De as Attendant-in-Ordinary, Grand Commander of All Armies Within and Without, and Colonel Director of Convicts; the Pacifying General Murong Lin as Guards Grand General; the rest received appointments according to rank.
repairs.after: He appointed Kuruguan Wei Left Chief Clerk, Duan Chong Right Chief Clerk, and Zhang Chong Dragon-Prancing General; he made Feng Heng, Administrator of Zhongshan, Minister of Personnel; Murong De Palace Attendant, Commander of All Armies Within and Without, and concurrently Colonel-Director of Retainers; and the Pacifying General Murong Lin Grand General of the Guards. The rest received appointments according to rank.
repairs.reason: 庫辱官 is the compound surname Kuruguan; only Feng Heng is made 吏部尚書; 司隸校尉 is Colonel-Director of Retainers.
repairs.authorReason: 庫辱官 is Kuruguan's compound surname; only 中山尹封衡 is made 吏部尚書, and 司隸校尉 is Colonel-Director of Retainers. The current grouping wrongly makes all four men one minister.

repairs.before: He appointed his left chief clerk Guan Wei of Ku Ruo, right chief clerk Duan Chong, dragon-cavalry commander Zhang Chong, and the governor of Zhongshan Feng Heng as Minister of the Civil Office; Murong De as Attendant-in-Ordinary, commander of all armies inside and outside the realm, and colonel of the masters of writing; the Pacifying General Murong Lin as Grand General of the Guards; and the remainder received posts according to merit.
repairs.after: He appointed Kuruguan Wei Left Chief Clerk, Duan Chong Right Chief Clerk, and Zhang Chong Dragon-Prancing General; he made Feng Heng, Governor of Zhongshan, Minister of Personnel; Murong De Palace Attendant, Commander of All Armies Inside and Outside, and concurrently Colonel-Director of Retainers; and the Pacifying General Murong Lin Grand General of the Guards. The rest received posts by rank.
repairs.reason: Parallel idiomatic: Kuruguan Wei; Feng Heng alone is Minister of Personnel; office grouping corrected.
repairs.authorReason: The existing proposal correctly fixes Kuruguan and 司隸校尉 but still misgroups all four preceding men as Minister of Personnel; the Chinese assigns 吏部尚書 to Feng Heng alone.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 中山尹封衡為吏部尚書

repairs.before: The Erudites Liu Xiang and Dong Mi argued that Yao's mother held the third rank among consorts, that the honored tomb was not Jiang Yuan's, making clear that the way of sage-kings put supreme impartiality first.
repairs.after: The Erudites Liu Xiang and Dong Mi argued that Yao's mother occupied the third rank among the consorts and did not use her honored status to outrank Jiang Yuan, showing that the way of sage-kings puts perfect impartiality first.
repairs.reason: 陵 is verbal ("overtop/outrank"), not a tomb.
repairs.authorReason: 不以貴陵薑嫄 means she did not rely on honored status to overtop Jiang Yuan; 陵 is a verb here, not a tomb.

repairs.before: The erudites Liu Xiang and Dong Mi argued that the mother of Yao ranked only third among consorts and that the honored tomb was not that of Jiang Yuan, showing that the way of sage-kings put supreme impartiality above birth and rank.
repairs.after: The erudites Liu Xiang and Dong Mi argued that Yao's mother ranked only third among the consorts and did not use her honored status to outrank Jiang Yuan, showing that the way of sage-kings put perfect impartiality first.
repairs.reason: Parallel idiomatic: 陵 is verbal.
repairs.authorReason: 陵 is verbal ('overstep/outrank'), so the clause is not about an honored tomb.
